Mr. Wickham was so thoroughly satisfied with their conversation that he never troubled himself, or irritated his dear sister-in-law Elizabeth, by raising the subject again. She was glad she had said enough to silence him.

Soon the day came for him and Lydia to leave. Mrs. Bennet had to accept a separation likely to last at least a year, since her husband firmly rejected her plan for the entire family to go to Newcastle.

'Oh, my dear Lydia,' she cried, 'when will we see each other again?'

'Oh goodness, I don't know. Perhaps not for two or three years.'

'Write to me often, dear.'

'As often as I can. But married women never have much time for letters, you know. My sisters can write to me. They'll have nothing else to do.'

Mr. Wickham said goodbye much more affectionately than his wife. He smiled, looked handsome, and delivered many charming compliments.

'He's as fine a fellow as I've ever met,' Mr. Bennet said once they had left. 'He simpers and smirks and flirts with the whole family. I'm enormously proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to produce a more valuable son-in-law.'

Missing her daughter left Mrs. Bennet low-spirited for several days.

'I often think,' she said, 'that nothing is worse than saying goodbye to the people we love. Life feels so lonely without them.'

'That's what happens when a daughter marries, Mother,' Elizabeth replied. 'It ought to make you happier that your other four daughters are still single.'

'Nothing of the kind. Lydia isn't leaving because she's married. She's leaving because her husband's regiment happens to be stationed far away. If it were closer, she wouldn't have gone so soon.'

Before long, however, fresh news lifted her spirits and filled her again with restless hope. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been ordered to prepare for her master's arrival. He was coming in a day or two and intended to spend several weeks shooting there. Mrs. Bennet could hardly sit still. She kept looking at Jane, smiling, and shaking her head.

'Well, well, so Mr. Bingley's coming, sister,' she said, for Mrs. Philips had brought the news first. 'Well, all the better. Not that I care, of course. He's nothing to us, you know, and I certainly never want to see him again. Still, he's perfectly welcome to come to Netherfield if it pleases him.'

He then bowed and left. He saw nobody in the street at the time. It is a quiet, deserted side street.

"William Bird, a tailor, states that he joined the group entering the house. He is English and has lived in Paris for two years. He was among the first to climb the stairs and heard the arguing voices. The harsh voice belonged to a Frenchman. He understood several words but cannot now recall them all. He distinctly heard 'sacré' and 'mon Dieu.' At the same time there was a scraping, scuffling noise, as though several people were struggling. The high-pitched voice was extremely loud, louder than the harsh one. He is certain it was not an Englishman's. It sounded German and might have belonged to a woman. He does not understand German.

"Four previously named witnesses were recalled. They stated that when the group reached the room containing Mademoiselle L.'s body, its door was locked from within. There was complete silence: no groaning or any other sound. After forcing the door open, they saw nobody. The windows in both the front and back rooms were shut and firmly secured on the inside. The connecting door was closed but unlocked. The door between the front room and the passage was locked, with its key inside. At the front of the fourth floor, at the end of the passage, a small room stood open, its door ajar. Old beds, boxes, and other objects filled it. These were carefully removed and examined. Every inch of the house was thoroughly searched. Chimney sweeps were sent through the chimneys in both directions. The building had four storeys and attic rooms. A roof trapdoor was securely nailed shut and appeared not to have been opened for years. Witnesses gave differing estimates of the interval between hearing the dispute and breaking into the room: some said only three minutes, others as many as five. Opening the door required considerable effort.

"Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker, states that he lives in the Rue Morgue and was born in Spain. He was among those who entered the house but did not go upstairs. He has a nervous disposition and feared the effects of becoming agitated. He heard the voices arguing. The harsh voice was French, though he could not distinguish the words. The high-pitched voice belonged to an Englishman; of that he is certain.

Watching him in these moods, I often reflected on the old philosophy of the divided soul, amusing myself by imagining two Dupins: one creative, the other analytical.

Do not assume from this that I am recounting some mystery or writing a fantastic tale. What I have described in my French friend was simply the effect of an overstimulated, perhaps even unhealthy, intellect. An example will best convey the nature of his remarks at such times.

One night we were walking along a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. Apparently absorbed in our own thoughts, we had said nothing for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin spoke:

'He's certainly a very small man, and he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.'

'Without a doubt,' I answered automatically. So deep in thought was I that I failed at first to notice how extraordinarily his comment fitted my reflections. A moment later I came to myself and felt profound amazement.

'Dupin,' I said seriously, 'I cannot understand this. I freely admit I'm astonished and can scarcely trust my senses. How could you possibly know I was thinking of—?' I stopped, wanting to establish beyond doubt that he really knew whom I meant.

'Of Chantilly,' he replied. 'Why stop? You were thinking that his small stature made him unsuitable for tragedy.'

That was exactly what had occupied my mind. Chantilly had formerly repaired shoes in the Rue St. Denis. Becoming obsessed with the stage, he had attempted the part of Xerxes in Crébillon's tragedy of that name and been publicly ridiculed for his performance.

'For heaven's sake,' I cried, 'explain the method—if there is one—that let you read so deeply into my mind.' In truth, I was even more shaken than I cared to admit.

'The fruit seller,' my friend answered, 'led you to conclude that this repairer of soles lacked the height for Xerxes and characters of that kind.'

'The fruit seller! You amaze me. I don't know any fruit seller.'

'The man who collided with you when we turned into this street, perhaps fifteen minutes ago.'

I now remembered a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples on his head. As we turned from the Rue C—— into the street where we now stood, he had accidentally almost knocked me over. But I could not imagine what that incident had to do with Chantilly.
